Last night\'s look, the research behind it, and the model.

If it would help, pick one thing
One thing to make or do (mastery)
A 90-second moment, if you would like one
You were on %1$s for %2$s — note anything?
Chosen apps stop interrupting you; their notifications wait quietly and arrive together at 8:00, 12:30 and 18:00. Conversations, calls and alarms always come through instantly.
Grant notification access to enable batching
When the batches arrive. The default three follow the trial this is drawn from, not anything about your day — move them to where you can actually take an interruption.
One calm summary per batch of held notifications.
Without this, the launcher never appears. One tap.
Could not check. Try again later.
Nothing here. When batching is on, held notifications collect in this journal so nothing is ever lost.
Android is letting these times drift by up to an hour to save battery. If you want them kept exactly, this phone can allow it.
A quiet landscape under the sky. Even a brief glance at greenery or water measurably steadies attention, so this is drawn to be looked at — and never to move.

If you write down a few small things that help you, one of them is offered — beside the app, never instead of it — at the moment you reach for something else. Only your words, never ours. Nothing is offered on a fourth reach in ten minutes, or during your quiet hours: those are not moments to be asked whether you have tried going for a walk.

If you write down a few short phrases in your own words — \"may I be kind to myself\" is the template, not the script — one of them is offered in the friction prompt. Your words only; never the launcher\'s. Neff 2003.
May I be kind to myself
Your plan: “If I’m about to %1$s, then I’ll %2$s.”

These are ones you have gone through every time. That might mean the pause has become scenery, or it might mean it is quietly doing its job and you genuinely wanted to go in. Only you know which. Nothing changes unless you change it.
%1$s — shown %2$d times, and you went in every time.
You have not named anything yet. You do not have to.

On its own, the pause only appears when you open an app from this screen. Tapping a notification, swiping through recents or following a link goes straight in — which is most of how a phone actually gets used. Turning this on means the pause applies however you arrive.

Android calls this an accessibility service, and that sounds worse than it is. It is set up so it cannot read your screen — not messages, not passwords, not what you are looking at. It is told the name of the app that came to the front, and nothing else. Android enforces that, not us.
On. The pause applies however you open an app.
Off. The pause only applies from this screen.
Lets the pause apply when you open an app from a notification or from recents, not just from the home screen.

MindAnchor uses this to notice when an app you have chosen a pause for comes to the front, so the pause works however you opened it. It cannot read your screen — only the name of the app that arrived.

Through your quiet hours the phone goes priority-only: starred contacts and repeat callers still reach you, everything else waits for morning. Set the hours to your night, not to a default — shift work and being on call are the norm, not the exception.
When you are most awake. The wind-down window starts from here unless you have already picked your own times.
Grant Do Not Disturb access to enable sunset
Wind down through the quiet hours

This counts and does not interpret. It compares your nights to your own usual — not to anybody else\'s, and not to a norm — and tells you the number. What it means is yours to say; phones are not good at that part and this one does not try.
You got to sleep well after your usual on %1$d of the last few nights.

Once a night, while the phone is charging and you are not using it, this compares the day against your own usual and pulls up what the research says the thing measured actually is. It never joins those two together — what a change means is yours to say.
Nothing yet. There will be something once there are enough days to compare against.
Nothing stood out. That is the usual answer and it is a good one.
Not yet looking for patterns across your days — that needs about four weeks of nights and check-ins together.
%1$s was higher than your usual — %2$s against about %3$s.
%1$s was lower than your usual — %2$s against about %3$s.
%1$s was later than your usual — %2$s against about %3$s.
%1$s was earlier than your usual — %2$s against about %3$s.
No matching research on file for this one.
These are counts from your own history, next to what the research says the thing counted is. Nothing here knows what it means about you.
Written on this phone, by a small model, from the passages below.
What your days have tended to do
Of the %1$d days when your %2$s was closest to last night\'s, %3$s came out lower than your usual.
Of the %1$d days when your %2$s was closest to last night\'s, %3$s came out higher than your usual.
That is a count of your own past days, not a forecast. It says nothing about how today will go, and nothing about why.

Every report shows you what the research says the thing measured actually is, drawn from a small set of passages that ships with the app. You can add more from a file on this phone — the more there is on file, the better the match to what your report is about.
Passages are shown to you word for word. What you add is what you will read.
One passage per line: an id, a source, then the text, separated by tab characters. Lines starting with # are ignored.
Ignored %1$d rows that were not in this format.
That file held more than fits, so the rest was left out.
Nothing in that file could be read as research, so nothing was changed.
That file could not be read.

The paragraph above a report — see Last night\'s look — would be written on this phone, by a small language model, from the passages already shown to you. You can add that model here, as a single GGUF file.

With a model on file that fits this phone, the paragraph is written here overnight, on this device, by this app\'s own copy of a small inference engine. Nothing about it ever leaves the phone. If the model is too large to run in the background, nothing runs — the report simply appears without a paragraph, exactly as it does with no model at all.
This phone has room to run it, with room to spare.
This phone can run it, but it is a tight fit — a busy night could still cost it.
This model is too large to run in the background on this phone.
This phone is flagged as low on memory, so no model is offered on it, at any size.
Add a model from a file
That file could not be copied.
Download started. MindAnchor will prompt you when the file has landed.
The system refused the download. Check the network or storage and try again.
Phi-4 mini downloaded. Use this as the narrate model?

The Phi-4 mini model was the v0.23.0–v0.25.6 way of writing a daily letter on this phone. The recommended path is now Settings → Reading → Daily letter (LLM), which uses a cloud model and a calmer voice. Letters already written by Phi-4 load and read back unchanged.
Nothing arrived that day — no reading, no wearable data, no check-in.
never — it runs overnight while charging, or on the button below
Each signal, how many of the last three months\' days have a value on file, and where the latest one came from. A signal missing here is a fact worth knowing, never a silent gap.
Nothing counted yet. Build last night\'s look once, under Reading, and this fills in.
from your wearable, via Health Connect
What arrived from the watch yesterday?
Read straight from Health Connect, just now:
Each reading is kept on this phone and feeds the nightly look.

A couple of taps, a few times a day, at times that move around so you cannot see them coming. This is the part that teaches the app what your own normal looks like — without it there is nothing to compare anything to. It asks less once it has learned enough, and you can skip any of them.
How does it feel right now?
It has enough to work with, so it asks less now.

Many watches measure heart-rate variability and never hand it over — it stays inside the maker\'s own app, and it cannot be worked out from heart rate alone. So this measures it directly, from your fingertip. It also means it still works if you change watch, or aren\'t wearing one.

Rest your index finger over the rear camera and the flash, covering both. Hold still, breathe normally, and stay off the phone for about 90 seconds. Sitting, before you get up, is the most comparable time of day.
Resting HRV %1$d ms, heart rate %2$d bpm.
That reading was too noisy to trust, so it has been thrown away rather than saved. Usually it is finger pressure — cover the lens and the flash completely, but rest the finger rather than pressing.
MindAnchor can estimate your sleep window from when the screen goes quiet at night — on this phone only, no wearable, nothing uploaded. Consistency matters more than hours.
Grant usage access to see your rhythm
Not enough nights recorded yet. Check back in a few days.
This is an estimate of how consistent your nightly phone-quiet window is — regular timing, not total hours, is what the research links to better mood and sleep.
From your last %1$d nights, your nights cluster around %2$s. A wind-down at %3$s would land an hour and a half before that.
Set MindAnchor as your home screen
Nothing hidden. Long-press any app to hide it from the drawer — it stays reachable by typing its exact name.
A calmer phone, built from published research. No accounts, no server — everything stays on this device. You choose what turns on; nothing is imposed.
What pulls at you? Pick what fits.
Apps I open without meaning to
My phone keeps me up at night
I want to know if any of this helps
Your plan — switch each on when ready:
• Notification batching (settings): chosen apps go quiet and arrive together three times a day. People always come through.
• Long-press any app and choose \"Add a pause\" — a breath and an intention before it opens.
• Sunset mode + sleep rhythm (settings): priority-only nights and a view of how regular your sleep is.
• The wellbeing pulse (settings): a 2-minute check-in every two weeks, scored honestly.
Explore at your own pace — every feature lives in settings and long-press menus, all off by default.
What fits? Pick what helps, skip what doesn\'t.
Both questions are optional. Whatever you skip, the launcher leaves off. You can change either one in settings.
At my best in the evening, asleep after midnight
I work shifts and sleep during the day
• Wind-down default set for your hours: %1$s
A 2-minute WHO-5 check-in every two weeks. It keeps an honest record, in your own words and numbers, of whether any of this is helping — the reading of it stays yours.
How have the last two weeks felt?
Five statements, answered 0 (at no time) to 5 (all of the time). This is a self-check, not a diagnosis.
0 = at no time · 5 = all of the time
In the higher range. The WHO-5 is not a diagnosis — it is a check-in on the last two weeks. Trends over time are more useful than any single number.

In the lower range — the kind of result that often shows up under a lot of stress or strain. Not a diagnosis, and it does not mean anything is wrong with you. Your people and your plan are one tap away whenever you want them. If this has been going on for a couple of weeks or more, talking to a GP can be a useful next step.

In the lowest range the WHO describes — the level of well-being often seen in people who are going through a really hard time. The WHO-5 is not a diagnosis; only a clinician can make that call. Given how much you are carrying, it might be worth talking to someone you trust or a GP. Your people are one tap away.
A few items are unanswered. Save only when you have answered all five.
MindAnchor is a wellness tool, not a clinical service. A low reading does not mean you are unwell.
A meaningful lift from the one before.
A meaningful drop from the one before.
Two weeks since your last pulse
Somewhere to write down what helps, and the people you would want to talk to. Yours to fill in, whenever you feel like it.
Everything here works offline and stays on this phone. It reaches real people — it never tries to be one.
No one added yet. You can add the people you\'d actually call, below.
MindAnchor is a wellness tool, not a treatment, and not a medical device. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.

Three skills from dialectical behaviour therapy, the treatment with the strongest evidence for getting through emotional crises. They are for riding out the next few minutes — nothing more is being asked of you.
Stop. Take a step back. Observe what is happening, inside and around you. Proceed mindfully — pick the next small action, not the whole day.

Cold water on your face or hands. Intense movement for a minute. Paced breathing, out longer than in. Then relax each muscle group in turn. These change body chemistry fast when thinking alone will not.

The cold water and the hard movement both swing your heart rate on purpose. If you have a heart condition, an eating disorder, or are pregnant, skip those two and ask a doctor first. The paced breathing and the muscle relaxation are gentle, and they work on their own.
Name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, one you can taste. Slowly, out loud if you can.
Nothing written yet. A plan is easiest to write on a calm day, for a day that is not — that is the whole idea.
Thoughts, feelings or situations I notice first
What helps me on my own
Things I can do without anyone else
Where I can go, who I can be around
Places and people that take the edge off
What I want to stay for
What I can put away, and who can hold it
A number is what makes this callable. Add one to save this person.
These people are never batched and never held back by sunset mode — if they reach out, your phone tells you straight away.
This phone could not open a dialer. The number is %1$s — call it from your phone app, or ask someone near you to.

Everything else here can be walked through, which is usually right and useless on the nights it matters. If this phone is set up as its own guardian, the apps you chose a pause for become genuinely unopenable through the quiet hours — a decision made while calm, kept by the phone rather than by you.
This has to be granted once from a computer, on a phone with no accounts signed in — usually right after a factory reset. It is a high bar on purpose.
This phone is set up as its own guardian. Chosen apps close for the quiet hours.
Your phone app, messages, settings and this app are never suspended, whatever you choose.
Any suspended apps open again straight away. Getting this back later needs another factory reset, so it is worth being sure — but if you want it back, take it back.

A grey screen is the single most effective change measured in this field — not through willpower, but because colour is most of what makes a feed feel alive. Trials consistently find people put the phone down sooner without it.
Android will not let an app turn this on by itself, which is the right rule. Run this once from a computer with the phone plugged in, and it sticks through reboots:
Go grey through the quiet hours

This borrows Android\'s colour correction, so the two cannot both be on at once. Whatever correction you had set is put back when the grey screen goes off. If you rely on it during the day, you may still want to leave the night setting alone.

Nothing here is backed up to the cloud, on purpose — so a reset or lost phone would take your plan, your people, your check-ins and your readings with it. Save a copy somewhere you trust, and bring it back whenever you need to. Restoring only ever adds to what is already here.
Saved. Keep it somewhere only you can reach.
That file isn\'t a MindAnchor copy, or it came from a newer version. Nothing was changed.
Couldn\'t read or write that file. Nothing was changed.

MindAnchor is an open-source, research-backed launcher. It has no accounts, no server and no analytics — by default, your data never leaves this phone. The one opt-in exception is the COROS Training Hub bridge under Settings → Measuring: when you connect it, the launcher fetches HRV and resting heart rate from COROS, over an encrypted connection, with your COROS password held in this phone\'s secure Keystore. The connection is off until you turn it on. It is a wellness tool, not a medical device, and it is no substitute for talking to someone.

Blocks mobile-internet content during a window you set — Castelo 2025 found this is the single biggest sustained-attention gain the category offers. The first time you turn it on, your phone will ask once for a system permission; you can take it back any time.
Going Light needs a one-time system permission.
It blocks mobile-internet content during a window you choose. The system will ask once; you can take it back any time from settings.
This is a setting Android will not let an app grant to itself. It is on purpose; the bar keeps the setting safe.
A line or two, if you like
No check-ins yet. They appear here as you complete them.
Nothing here yet. Tap + to start.
Reset every note\'s type and run the on-device model over them again. Use this after upgrading the model, or if a note has the wrong type.
This resets every note\'s type and runs the on-device model over them again. It is slow — several minutes for a few hundred notes — and runs in the background; you can leave the screen.
Jot something down — it saves here, in order, with the time.
Nothing yet. The first line you write lands here.

MindAnchor can read heart rate, sleep, steps, exercise and mindfulness sessions from any watch or app that writes to Health Connect. The data never leaves this phone. You stay in control — grant or revoke each type from the system Health Connect screen at any time.
Checking what your watch is sharing…
Health Connect is not installed on this phone. Install it from the Play Store to bring your wearable data in.
No data is being read yet. Tap below to choose what to share.
Reading %1$d of %2$d signal types from your watch. Tap to change.
Couldn\'t open Health Connect. The app may be missing, disabled, or may not have responded in time. Check it is installed and enabled, then try again.
heart rate samples — used to show mean and resting heart rate
resting heart rate — used to show recovery from your usual
heart rate variability (HRV) — used alongside the camera PPG for a fuller recovery picture
sleep sessions — used for duration and timing
step count — used against the 7,000-step threshold from the steps-and-depression meta-analysis
exercise sessions — used for active minutes
calories burned — kept for future use; nothing reads it today
mindfulness sessions — used to surface practice time next to steps and sleep
What this app does NOT do
Write back to your watch or any other app. The launcher only reads.
Send anything off this phone. There is no network call to a server, ever.
Diagnose or interpret. The numbers are shown, not judged.

Some watches — COROS today — do not release every signal to Health Connect. This optional bridge fills the gaps. The launcher makes outbound calls to the COROS Training Hub (a third-party server) and stores your COROS email + password in this phone\'s secure Keystore for as long as the bridge stays connected. Disconnect wipes both. Off by default.

What goes to the COROS server: your email + password (for sign-in), the resulting access token, and the three data fetches (HRV, daily summary, activity list). What does not go anywhere else: nothing — this bridge is the only outbound channel and the launcher\'s promise of \"no other network call\" still holds.

Sign in once with your COROS Training Hub email + password. COROS requires the password as an MD5 hash, so that is what is sent, over an encrypted connection. The hash stands in for the password, so treat it with the same care.
Fetch the last 7 days of nightly HRV (RMSSD ms) and the last ~28 days of resting heart rate from the Training Hub every 6 hours.
Show the data on the wellness card, alongside the Health Connect data. Health Connect wins when both have a reading; COROS fills the gaps for the signals the watch does not release.
No analytics, no crash reports, no telemetry. The encrypted credential blob is the only thing on disk.
Does not sign out of the COROS phone app. The side-channel uses the Training Hub web API, not the mobile API, so your phone app stays signed in.

Your own history for each signal, shown in the same units your watch or ring writes. None of this is sent off the phone. None of it is compared to anyone else. The launcher never applies a population threshold to a person.
Still building a picture. Each signal needs 14 days of your own data before the baseline is honest enough to show. The home card and this section appear once it is.
The launcher reads from Health Connect and never writes back. The data never leaves this phone. The per-signal rolling history lives in app-private storage and is included in the on-device backup.
Written on this phone each morning by the same model that writes the nightly report. Tap any letter to read it.
A short letter, written each morning at the time you choose. Tap the notification to read it. The on-device Phi-4 model from earlier versions is still available as a legacy option — see below.
Send me a letter each morning
No letters yet. The first arrives at 8 AM, once enough days have passed.
No letters yet. Phi-4 isn\'t installed — open Settings → Model to install it.
This letter is no longer on the phone.
A letter is what your own data looked like to a model on this phone. It is not advice.
One letter a day. Yours alone.
Couldn\'t write the letter right now.
The launcher writes you one letter a day, in its own voice.
How large the text reads on the letter. Large is the largest size that still fits every letter without clipping or hiding controls.

Want the daily letter? It is written by a small AI, in the launcher\'s own voice. You will need a free key from Groq — sign-up takes about 2 minutes at console.groq.com. Paste the key below, then tap Test connection.

A second, automatic copy in your own Google Drive — encrypted before it leaves this phone, in two text files (notes and letters). The app can only see files it created; the rest of your Drive is invisible.
Backed up. The remote copy is encrypted with the same key as the local backup.
Couldn\'t back up right now. Will retry on the next entry.
Couldn\'t sign in. Check the account picker and try again.
Forgot the account. The remote copy is still in your Drive; turn the bridge back on any time.
